title: POC Weekly - Latency Tuning (NovaPay)
summary: Weekly POC sync focusing on tail token-first-time (TTFT), streaming behavior, sequence length distribution, and kernel selection tradeoffs. SE shared fresh benchmark results showing 12% TTFT improvement with streaming and 8k kv-cache tweaks; discussed remaining outliers at 99th percentile and suggested targeted kernel profiles for long sequences. Agreed next steps: run a 2k-request benchmark with streaming enabled, customer to share representative prompt set and sequence histogram, AE to send updated Dedicated pricing options and proposed timeline for a canary using dedicated pool.
next_steps: Marco to run 2k inference benchmark with streaming enabled and share results by 2026-07-16
Jillian to send updated pricing/options for dedicated pool and a proposed canary timeline by 2026-07-20
NovaPay to provide 100 representative prompts and sequence length histogram by 2026-07-18
Schedule follow-up deep dive on kernel profiles (SE-led) for 2026-07-21
action_items: Marco Diaz | Run 2k inference benchmark with streaming enabled (measure cold TTFT and 95/99 pctiles) | 2026-07-16
Jillian Park | Share Dedicated pool pricing and sample SLA for canary | 2026-07-20
Anita Rao | Upload 100 representative prompts + sequence length histogram to shared drive | 2026-07-18
Tom Benson | Share infra limits (max concurrent connections, egress) for canary planning | 2026-07-19
questions: Is streaming acceptable for our user latency SLOs or do we need sub-200ms TTFT?
Can we tolerate higher token cost for longer sequences if latency improves?
What kernel profile is best for mixed short+long traffic?
header: Date: 2026-07-14 | Time: 15:00 UTC | Duration: 45m | Recording: auto
transcript:
[00:00] Jillian: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we got the usual AE+SE pair today, Jillian and Marco from Redwood. Hi all.
[00:12] Anita: Hi Jillian, hi Marco, thanks, we got Tom and Liam on as well.
[00:16] Tom: Hi.
[00:18] Liam: Hey.
[00:22] Marco: Quick agenda: share the latest latency runs, go over TTFT and streaming numbers, discuss long-sequence kernel choices, then next steps. Sound good?
[00:32] Anita: Yep that sounds good. We're mainly seeing the 95th and 99th spikes which are hurting UX for some flows.
[00:39] Marco: Right, so quick context: last week we tuned batch sizes and enabled prefix KV cache. This week we tried enabling streaming with early token flush and switched kernel profile to the mixed-long optimized kernels for 8k sequences.
[00:54] Jillian: I'll let Marco walk the numbers but high level we saw a TTFT drop on average and some outliers still persist.
[01:03] Marco: Ok numbers: baseline (no streaming, default kernels) — median TTFT 160ms, 95th 420ms, 99th 880ms. With streaming enabled plus kv-cache warm we measured median 140ms, 95th 360ms, 99th 760ms. So roughly 12% median improvement and about 10-14% improvement on tails.
[01:26] Anita: Those are promising. Is the 99th still from cold starts or long sequences?
[01:31] Marco: Mostly long sequences plus a few cold-worker misses. We saw a cluster around 6k-8k sequences where kernels switch and the performance cliff happens. Also some cold TTFTs where the GPU wasn't primed — I think your traffic has heavy long tail.
[01:47] Liam: Quick question, when you say kernel switch, is that the Triton kernel selector or something at inference runtime?
[01:53] Marco: It's our runtime choosing optimized kernels — small-attn kernels for short seqs, and alternative fused kernels for long seqs. The selector looks at seq length distribution at request time. Sometimes it misclassifies near the boundary and you get a fallback path that's slower.
[02:07] Tom: We do have a mixed workload, some requests are 128 tokens, some are 6k text.
[02:11] Jillian: Right, and that's the classic padding vs dynamic batching debate. If you can give us the seq length histogram we can recommend a mix of kernel profiles and maybe a route policy: short requests go to low-latency pool, long requests to cost-optimized pool.
[02:28] Anita: We can provide the histogram, yes. Also curious about streaming — do we lose quality/ordering if we stream partial tokens?
[02:35] Marco: Good question — streaming doesn't change the model output aside from token emission timing. We flush tokens as they're generated; for chat-like outputs streaming is great. For some complex structured outputs you might want to wait for end-of-sequence. But quality is unchanged.
[02:51] Anita: Ok.
[02:54] Marco: Another note: TTFT cold starts improved when we increased warm workers for the canary, but that increases cost. We suggested a hybrid: keep a small warm pool sized for your peak short request QPS and autoscale long-worker pool for long sequences.
[03:09] Liam: What's the size of 'small warm pool' in your test?
[03:12] Marco: In the benchmark we kept 4 warm workers per GPU; that cut cold TTFTs by ~200ms on average but cost went up roughly 8%.
[03:21] Jillian: Tradeoffs to consider: user SLO vs cost. We can model cost impact once you give traffic profile.
[03:28] Anita: Sounds good. Anything about quantization effects? We test 4-bit in prod.
[03:33] Marco: We ran both 4-bit and 8-bit profiles. 4-bit gave slightly faster kernel compute but some pathing changes made longer sequences more variable. 8-bit is more stable on tails. So if your workloads have a significant 6k-plus tail, 8-bit on those workers gave more consistent 99th percentile.
[03:53] Tom: So could we run mixed quantization — 4-bit for short pool, 8-bit for long pool?
[03:59] Marco: Exactly, that's one configuration we recommend. You can route short seqs to 4-bit low-latency workers and long seqs to 8-bit high-memory workers.
[04:09] Anita: Nice.
[04:12] Marco: Regarding kernel choices, the mixed-long fused kernels perform best at >4k tokens but there's a warmup overhead the first time a kernel is JIT-ed on a worker. That contributes to cold TTFTs too.
[04:26] Liam: Is JIT overhead avoidable?
[04:28] Marco: We can pre-jit kernels on boot and keep them resident; that increases startup time but avoids first-request spikes. It's an ops decision.
[04:36] Jillian: Quick pause — any blockers from NovaPay side for the next run?
[04:40] Anita: We need to gather the prompt set and histogram, and confirm whether we want streaming for payment-flow UX. Also legal wants to check data retention but that's a separate thread.
[04:51] Jillian: Understood. We'll keep the security docs thread separate. Marco, can you describe the benchmark you'll run?
[04:56] Marco: Sure. Plan: synthetic 2k requests reflecting your short/long split — we'll run with streaming on, collect cold TTFTs by restarting workers between runs, and measure median/95/99 plus tokens per second and cost estimate. We'll run both mixed quantization and fixed 8-bit and present comparisons.
[05:12] Anita: If you're restarting workers to measure cold TTFTs, can you also include a warm-run baseline?
[05:18] Marco: Yes we'll include warm-run numbers.
[05:20] Tom: For the canary, what's a safe ramp plan?
[05:23] Jillian: We typically suggest canary at 5-10% of traffic, run for 48 hours, then 25% for another day if stable. For Dedicated pool we can pin GPUs to avoid noisy neighbors.
[05:36] Tom: Any SLA differences if we go Dedicated?
[05:38] Jillian: Dedicated gives you more predictable tail latency and throughput and optional SLA. We'll send pricing and the canary timeline after this call.
[05:46] Anita: Great.
[05:48] Marco: Also note we observed a specific regression with your prompt that includes many short system messages — that bunched tokens and formed a longer effective sequence because of system role concatenation. Might be worth normalizing prompts to reduce artificial length.
[06:03] Anita: Good catch, we can look into that.
[06:07] Liam: On infra, we have a soft limit of 200 concurrent connections per cluster node; will that affect batching?
[06:15] Marco: It can. If concurrency is constrained you'll see more batching which helps throughput but can increase TTFT for individual requests. We'll factor that into the model.
[06:25] Jillian: Ok I'm going to recap actions then open for any last questions.
[06:29] Marco: Wait one more datapoint — we measured streaming flush interval tuning: shrinking flush interval from 50ms to 20ms improved perceived TTFT for short replies but increased token RPCs by ~6%. So a small cost tradeoff for perceived latency.
[06:44] Anita: If it's only 6% token overhead that's probably acceptable.
[06:48] Tom: Depends on volume but likely acceptable for payment-flow confirmations.
[06:53] Jillian: Recap: Marco runs the 2k benchmark with streaming + mixed quantization and shares numbers by Friday; Anita provides prompts/histogram; Jillian sends pricing and canary plan. Any other blockers?
[07:06] Anita: None from me.
[07:09] Liam: all good.
[07:10] Jillian: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up in email and schedule the kernel deep dive for next week. Bye.
[07:16] (meeting ends)
notes: Benchmark showed ~12% median TTFT improvement with streaming
99th percentile driven by long sequences and cold JIT/warmup overhead
Recommendation: dual pool (short low-latency 4-bit, long stable 8-bit) with routing policy; pre-jit kernels on boot for long-pool to avoid first-request spikes
Streaming flush interval can be tuned (20-50ms) to trade perceived TTFT vs token RPC cost
